item.content:encoded:
The Tonga Family Health Association ( TFHA ) has marked International Humanitarian Day in Nuku'alofa today with a focus on strengthening community resilience and ensuring humanitarian action upholds justice, dignity and equity.

TFHA executive director, Pelenatita Longopa, said the day called attention to the rising threats and attacks against aid workers and civilians, while calling for an end to impunity for violations of international humanitarian law.

Through its SPRINT IV Project, TFHA has positioned sexual and reproductive health ( SRH ) as a critical humanitarian priority, particularly during disasters when essential services can be disrupted or overlooked.

TFHA 's humanitarian work includes providing women, girls and vulnerable groups with access to mental health care, contraception and protection from gender-based violence.

Pelenatita Longopa said SRH was central to resilience because it protected the health and dignity of families during crises, empowered women and young people to participate in recovery and strengthened coordination between health, protection and communities.

Community representatives and humanitarians said humanitarian preparedness was a lived reality for Tonga, with the country's experience of volcanic eruptions and cyclones demonstrating the need for community-driven resilience.

The Civil Society Forum of Tonga also received donated humanitarian supplies from UN Global Medics, including hygiene packs and a water purifier intended to support families during future disasters.

The second half of the event featured a roundtable discussion involving humanitarian workers, volunteers, non-government organisations representatives and community members.

Discussions focused on how communities experienced and remembered the 2022 Hunga Tonga-Hunga Ha'apai volcanic eruption, including humanitarian challenges faced during the response.

Participants also examined lessons from the response, including what worked well, gaps in humanitarian coordination and challenges faced by agencies and communities.

The discussion also looked at the way forward, including how communities and service providers could strengthen disaster preparedness and resilience through strategic planning.

item.title: NZ fur seal stranded on remote Ha'apai island released at sea
item.description: A New Zealand fur seal that was stranded in a remote island in Ha'apai has been released at sea after spending four days in the care of a local fisherman. The rare visitor came ashore on Tokulu, a small limestone island located between the remote islands of Tungua and Nomuka.
item.content:encoded:
A New Zealand fur seal that was stranded in a remote island in Ha'apai has been released at sea after spending four days in the care of a local fisherman.

The rare visitor came ashore on Tokulu, a small limestone island located between the remote islands of Tungua and Nomuka.

Fisherman Sione Meiha’amoa (Toa) told Matangi Tonga that he discovered the juvenile seal stranded on Tokulu last Wednesday, 12 August, and brought it back to his home island of Tungua.

" I found it stranded ashore on Tokulu," Toa said.

The seal remained inland for four days while Toa cared for it before it was released at sea on Sunday, 16 August, to continue its journey.

Toa said a group from New Zealand was contacted through the Prime Minister’s Office to assess the seal. He understood from the group that the animal was about one year old and still a juvenille. He was also told that it had come from New Zealand.

" They were concerned for the animal and wanted me to release it."

Toa said he was told he could face a fine of $10,000 pa'anga if he did not release the seal.

The young fur seal has now been returned to the sea, with hopes that it will make its way back towards its natural habitat.

New Zealand fur seals are not naturally found in Tonga, where tropical waters are far outside the species' usual cold and temperate habitat.

Sightings of seals in Tonga are rare, although similar unusual appearances have been recorded in Tonga, Fiji, Cook Islands, and Tahiti over the years.

The unusual arrival comes as Tonga has experienced periods of colder-than-usual weather in recent months.

The New Zealand Department of Conservation ( DOC ) website states that Kekeno are the most common seals in New Zealand and their population is growing. They are usually found on rocky shores throughout mainland New Zealand, the Chatham Islands, and the subantarctic islands, as well as parts of Australia .

Seals are very good swimmers and weaned pups will sometimes travel great distances. On land seals have been found in unusual places such as backyards, drains and streets.

“Despite these odd appearances, seals are best left alone with no human intervention.”

Fur seals and sea lions are distinguished from other seals by their external ear flaps and hind flippers which rotate forward, allowing them to move quickly on land.

New Zealand fur seals can be distinguished from sea lions by their pointy nose and smaller size.

This pointy-nosed seal has long pale whiskers and a body covered with two layers of fur. Their coat is dark grey-brown on the back, and lighter below.

Adult females grow to a maximum length 1.5 m, weight 30-50 kg, while adult males grow to amaximum length 2.5 m, weight 90-150 kg.

From birth to weaning Pups are suckled for about 300 days, though some will continue to suckle into their second year. During spring most pups are weaned and disperse. Juvenile fur seals have been found over 1000 km away from their place of birth.

item.title: Prop idol has his 'mojo' back - and Wallabies want more
item.description: Wallabies coach Les Kiss will stay in regular touch with Taniela Tupou's French club to ensure the in-form prop remains a regular fixture. Les Kiss will continue to assure Taniela Tupou's new French bosses the Wallabies are looking after him, thrilled how the prop has rediscovered his "mojo" in the Test arena.
item.content:encoded:
Wallabies coach Les Kiss will stay in regular touch with Taniela Tupou's French club to ensure the in-form prop remains a regular fixture.

Les Kiss will continue to assure Taniela Tupou's new French bosses the Wallabies are looking after him, thrilled how the prop has rediscovered his "mojo" in the Test arena.

Tupou scored two first-half tries for Australia, who trailed before scoring 42 consecutive points in a 56-17 defeat of Japan in Townsville on Saturday.

All three starting front-rowers, as well as replacement hooker Brandon Paenga-Amosa and back-rowers Harry Wilson and Charlie Cale, were Australia's try-scorers in Townsville.

Tupou scored the match-winner in Osaka against Eddie Jones' men a week earlier after coming off the bench and has shown power and skill to indicate he's back near his best approaching next year's home Rugby World Cup.

" He's found a little bit of himself again, and he's been more of himself," Wallabies coach Kiss said, while also noting his combination with good mate and returning lock Lukhan Salakaia-Loto.

" I'm very, very big on making sure the players be themselves as much as possible."

Former Queensland Reds star Tupou agonised over his move from Australian rugby to France, with Racing 92 last season but it's helped him turn back the clock after several underwhelming seasons at the Melbourne Rebels and NSW Waratahs.

" Moving to France, he's found out who he is a little bit more and he's come back and he's really connected with the group here and found that bit of mojo that he likes to thrive on," Kiss said.

With English-based Tom Hooper yet to return to the side, Tupou is the only overseas-based Wallaby currently in the Test rotation.

The coach has remained in touch with Racing 92's staff to ensure they have his services for the two-Test tour of Argentina that begins later this month and hopefully beyond.

" All good, as I believe, at this stage.

" I'll be talking to the coach and the team manager of Racing, this week, again, to make sure they understand how we're looking after Nella and making sure we're doing the right thing with him and working him hard.

" So they can trust the process as well. But, yeah, he'll be with us."

Jones joked post-game that Tupou played as if there was a pizza on offer for every try and reckoned he would even deliver one to the change-rooms himself.

" No pizza, I'll have to hit him up about that one," Tupou grinned.

" I've got a lot of love and respect for Eddie, actually. Nothing against that, he loves me, I know that."

Tupou said he wanted to "take it to the next level" after finding his feet in France.

And he said Kiss's tweaks were helping him get there.

" To get the ball in my hands as a forward, less running without the ball, more running with it," Tupou said.

" We're still working on it, but it's good to see forwards scoring tries."
